title: Acute Severe Headache with Fever and Neck Stiffness (Bacterial Meningitis)
patient_instructions: You are a 22-year-old who came to the emergency department this morning because your head has been aching all over (forehead and both sides) since you woke up. It is 7-8/10, dull, constant and getting worse; painkillers have not helped. This is the first time you have had a headache like this. If asked: you feel FEVERISH, your NECK is SORE and stiff, bright light hurts your eyes (photophobia) and you feel nauseated but have not vomited. There is NO rash. It did NOT come on like a sudden thunderclap or as the 'worst headache of your life' in seconds. No recent head injury, no weakness, no numbness, no blurred vision. You are sexually active. You feel unwell and frightened. Ideas: you think you may have 'a bad flu' but are scared it is something serious. Concerns: 'Could this be meningitis?' Expectations: you want to be assessed quickly and feel better. Act mildly drowsy and uncomfortable; hold your neck stiffly.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor on duty in a rural district hospital emergency department. A 22-year-old presents with a severe headache that began this morning. In 8 minutes: take a focused history and state the examination findings you would seek, give your most likely diagnosis, and outline your immediate emergency management. Speak your actions aloud so the examiner can follow your plan.
examiner_instructions: This is an emergency station - reward recognition that this is a time-critical, must-not-miss presentation. Award marks for a focused SIQORAA headache history that screens the key differentials (SAH, meningitis, ICH, brain tumour, migraine, tension) and specifically elicits fever, neck stiffness, photophobia and nausea while excluding thunderclap onset. If the candidate asks for examination findings, provide: temperature 38.5 C, neck stiffness with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, no rash, normal fundoscopy and normal focal neurology. The critical safety points: give first-dose IV/IM antibiotics WITHOUT delay (do not wait for CT/LP), give dexamethasone before/with the first antibiotic dose, call 000/arrange retrieval, and notify public health (notifiable disease). Prompt once: 'What will you give, and when?' Mark communication for keeping the frightened, unwell patient informed.

criteria: Focused SIQORAA headache history establishing acute worsening bilateral headache
Screens serious differentials - SAH (thunderclap), ICH, tumour, infection
Elicits meningitis features: fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea; asks about rash
Requests relevant examination: temperature, Kernig/Brudzinski, fundoscopy, focal neurology, rash
States bacterial meningitis as most likely with supporting features
Gives sensible differentials (SAH, encephalitis, migraine, tension headache)
Notes Kernig/Brudzinski have low sensitivity - absence does not exclude
Recognises time-critical emergency - calls 000/retrieval and admits
Gives first-dose empirical IV/IM antibiotics (ceftriaxone 2 g) WITHOUT delaying for CT/LP
Adds dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose
States CT-before-LP indications and does not delay treatment
Notifies public health and arranges contact tracing/chemoprophylaxis
Keeps the frightened, unwell patient informed with clear plain-language explanation
Efficient, calm, empathetic approach appropriate to an emergency

red_flags: Non-blanching purpuric/petechial rash indicating meningococcaemia - give immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin/ceftriaxone before transfer
Reduced GCS, focal neurological deficit, papilloedema, seizure or immunocompromise - CT before LP, but never delay antibiotics
Thunderclap onset (worst headache in seconds) suggesting subarachnoid haemorrhage
Signs of sepsis/septic shock - hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental state requiring resuscitation
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG): empirical therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in adults is ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (add benzylpenicillin/amoxicillin for Listeria cover if age >50, immunocompromised or pregnant); do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG): dexamethasone 10 mg IV given just before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis

eTG community suspected meningococcaemia: immediate ceftriaxone 2 g (child >=1 month 50 mg/kg up to 2 g) IV/IM or benzylpenicillin 2.4 g (child 60 mg/kg up to 2.4 g) IV/IM, ideally after blood cultures but without delaying treatment

NSW Health / notifiable disease: invasive meningococcal disease is notifiable - notify the public health unit and arrange contact tracing and chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for close contacts
learning_objectives: Recognise bacterial meningitis as a must-not-miss cause of acute headache and act without delay
Prioritise first-dose parenteral antibiotics and dexamethasone over completing imaging in a rural setting
Apply CT-before-LP indications and understand the limits of Kernig/Brudzinski signs
Understand the public-health obligations for a notifiable meningococcal infection
key_points: In suspected bacterial meningitis, antibiotics must not wait for CT or LP - give the first dose immediately and transfer
Dexamethasone should be given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, not after
A non-blanching purpuric rash mandates immediate parenteral penicillin/ceftriaxone in the community before transfer
In a rural district hospital, stabilise and give first-dose antibiotics locally, then call 000/retrieval - do not wait for tertiary review

citations.claim: Meningitis is a time-critical, serious disorder that must not be missed and requires urgent recognition and treatment - consistent with the 000/transfer/immediate-antibiotic pathway.
Structuring the differential as probability diagnoses and serious disorders not to be missed follows the Murtagh diagnostic strategy model applied to a young patient with acute headache.
Efficiently acknowledging the patient's worry while keeping the acute assessment focused reflects patient-centred questioning.
